questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the core commitment established by the Truman Doctrine
questions.stem: A planner's memo on containment describes an announcement that committed the government to support free peoples resisting attempted subjugation and to aid states where armed minorities threatened them. What did that announcement establish?

options.text: That supporting peoples resisting coercion is a standing obligation, not a deal for one country
That the government would intervene wherever in the world a civil war happened to begin
options.misconception: Treats the doctrine as a blank cheque for intervention anywhere

options.text: That economic aid alone was certain to keep newly independent states free
options.misconception: Believes the doctrine promised aid with no political commitment

options.text: That action had to come only through a collective body of states rather than directly
options.misconception: Assumes the doctrine required action solely through a league

questions.explanation: The announcement framed support for peoples resisting coercion as a general and continuing commitment, so the aid to Greece and Turkey became an example of a policy. It promised neither automatic intervention everywhere nor aid without conditions.
questions.hint: Ask whether the promise was for one country or for a category.

The tonnage shows the airlift depended on ground convoys, so it was never really viable
options.misconception: Contradicts the memo's own account of the airlift

options.text: Because the tonnage was high, the blockade must already have been lifted at that point
options.misconception: Assumes tonnage figures reveal when a blockade ended

options.text: The comparison shows air freight cost less than trucking, so the airlift was also cheaper
options.misconception: Confuses physical feasibility with a cost claim never made

questions.explanation: Carrying the needed tonnage for months without any ground route shows the airlift could sustain the city's supplies against the blockade's pressure. Nothing in the comparison speaks to cost, and tonnage figures do not date the lifting of the blockade.
questions.hint: Focus on what the volume makes possible, not on cost.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of recovery aid paid directly to European governments
questions.stem: A planning memo tabulates aid figures for a European recovery program, showing that 13.3 billion dollars was committed over four years, of which 11.9 billion went to European governments. What share of the program went to European governments?

About 10 percent, since the remaining 1.4 billion is close to a tenth of the total
options.misconception: Reports the smaller share as though it were the main one

options.misconception: Guesses a round fraction without using the figures

options.misconception: Assumes an even split between recipients

questions.hint: Divide the 11.9 figure by the 13.3 total.

That every member must automatically use armed force in response to any attack at all
options.misconception: Reads a collective commitment as compulsory participation

options.misconception: Overreads the treaty as eliminating national defense

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a threat assessment was built and why it shaped policy
questions.stem: In a briefing memo, the planner explains how a 1950 assessment of Soviet capability and intent was constructed. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The assessment argued from a gap between American and Soviet capabilities, inferred Soviet intentions to be expansionist, and treated uncertainty about future Soviet behavior as itself dangerous, so a build-up now was presented as the cheapest form of insurance. That framing mattered because it made a large military program look like caution rather than aggression, and it supplied the argument that a defensive posture and an aggressive posture could be funded as the same thing.

questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies the capability comparison, the judgment about intent, and the treatment of uncertainty as danger. It should also connect that framing to the program of spending the report proposed.
questions.hint: Name the premises and then the conclusion they supported.

questions.learningObjective: Compare the authority behind majority and binding decisions
questions.stem: A city planning memo compares two procedures: the general assembly voted by a simple majority of those present, while the security council required concurring votes including that of its permanent members. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.text: The assembly could act by a simple majority because its votes were recommendations, not binding commands
The assembly's majority rule made its decisions as binding as the council's decisions were
options.misconception: Treats recommendations as carrying the same force as binding decisions

options.text: The difference shows the assembly actually held more power than the security council did
options.misconception: Infers power from voting procedure rather than from the mandate

options.text: The difference shows that smaller bodies are always more democratic than larger ones
options.misconception: Generalizes about body size rather than about the two mandates

questions.explanation: Because the assembly's resolutions recommended rather than commanded, a simple majority could express a collective view without binding member states, while the council's votes could commit the organization to action. The difference in power follows from the mandates, not from the size of the body.
questions.hint: Ask what each body's votes actually did.

That both countries had abandoned communist commitments entirely by the end of the decade

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the recovery program was justified as economic rather than military
questions.stem: In another briefing memo, the planner explains how a European recovery program was presented as an economic measure rather than a military one. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The program's designers argued that the region's problems were largely economic: destroyed capacity, disrupted trade, and unusable currencies left economies unable to buy what they needed. If recovery restored production and employment, they reasoned, the appeal of outside control would weaken on its own, so aid was framed as rebuilding rather than as buying allies. The framing also suited a preference for European governments to run their own programs, since a large American administration of every project would have cost more and provoked resistance.

questions.explanation: A strong answer states the economic diagnosis and links it to reduced political vulnerability, and it should note the preference for European-led administration. It should avoid describing the program as a military build-up in disguise.
questions.hint: State the diagnosis before the political conclusion.

questions.learningObjective: Compare collective defense commitments with national military autonomy
questions.stem: A city planner's memo weighs the alliance's collective defense article against the need for each member to keep its own forces. Which combined judgment is most accurate?

options.text: The treaty pooled responses to aggression while leaving each member to decide what help it would give

options.misconception: Turns a commitment of assistance into a unified command

options.text: The treaty made members independent of one another, since any one of them could refuse help
options.misconception: Reads discretionary assistance as complete independence

options.text: The treaty applied only to economic disputes arising between member states
options.misconception: Misstates the article as covering economic disputes

questions.hint: Ask what the article pooled and what it left open.

questions.stem: An assessment memo describes a 1950 document that assumed the Soviet Union was driven by long-term expansion and that its military capacity would keep growing. Which feature of that assessment most shaped later policy?

Assuming the Soviet Union harbored no long-term ambitions of any kind

options.misconception: Understates the assessment's actual conclusion

5.7 billion dollars, since adding the two figures gives the combined total

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the containment announcement reframed the problem of coercion
questions.stem: A briefing memo asks how the 1947 announcement changed the way governments under pressure were treated. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The announcement treated the problem as a general one, since subjugation by armed minorities or outside powers could be reversed if the people resisting it were supported. questions.explanation: A strong answer explains the shift from a country-by-country bargain to a stated general commitment and notes the effect on how other states expected to be treated. It should keep the two specific countries as examples of the policy.
questions.hint: Say what the announcement treated as a general problem.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the communist split altered the balance of power within the bloc
questions.stem: A briefing memo asks how the split between the two great powers changed the balance inside the communist world. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: For a decade the two countries spoke for one bloc, and disputes were settled inside a single hierarchy. When they began backing rival sides in the same wars and arguing publicly at the United Nations, the bloc's unity became a liability: smaller governments could play one side against the other, seek aid from both, and eventually leave the rivalry behind. The split also opened a space for states that had expected a single communist command to seek their own paths.

questions.explanation: A strong answer traces the shift from a single command to competing patrons and then to the room this gave smaller states. It should avoid claiming the split ended communist cooperation altogether.
questions.hint: Explain what smaller governments could now do.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the logic and the effects of a strategic threat assessment
questions.stem: The briefing memo asks the planner to explain the reasoning of a 1950 assessment and why it mattered for policy. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The assessment combined a comparison of present and projected capabilities with a judgment about Soviet intentions, then presented the resulting gap as urgent. questions.stem: A briefing memo explains how the announcement of 1947 changed the way later administrations treated requests for aid. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Because the announcement framed support for peoples resisting coercion as a general commitment, later administrations could treat aid to a new nation as the application of an existing policy rather than a fresh political argument each time. options.text: Both bodies took binding action on the conflict at the same moment
options.misconception: Claims simultaneous binding action by both bodies

options.text: The council, not the assembly, was the body that issued the condemnation
options.misconception: Reverses which body issued the condemnation

questions.explanation: The assembly could condemn the intervention with a large majority because its votes were recommendations, while the council could not act because a permanent member's veto blocked it. The contrast shows how the two mandates behaved under the same pressure.
questions.hint: Ask which body could speak and which could not decide.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the diplomatic opening created by a rival patron's split
questions.stem: An office note describes how the United States opened talks with Beijing in 1971 and established a relationship two years later. What does this illustrate?

options.text: A rivalry inside the communist bloc created openings for diplomacy by a government outside it
The United States had maintained close and continuous ties with Beijing for decades
options.misconception: Contradicts the chronology in the note

options.text: The United States forced the split open and dictated the terms of the reconciliation
options.misconception: Overstates American control over the other powers' quarrel

options.text: The United States was ready to recognize Beijing whatever the cost to its existing partners
options.misconception: Assumes recognition was costless to the existing alliance

questions.explanation: The timing of the talks shows the value of the split to an outside government: once the two communist powers were estranged, approaching one of them no longer meant siding against the other. The note does not support long-standing ties or American control of the quarrel.
questions.hint: Ask why the approach was possible only then.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Reason about a combined drive and flanking landing
questions.stem: The planner's file notes that a summer offensive pushed the front far below the parallel and that an amphibious landing was made well behind the advancing line. What does this suggest about the campaign's plan?

options.text: It combined a drive down the peninsula with a landing intended to cut the enemy's supply lines
The front never moved south of the parallel during the whole campaign
options.misconception: Contradicts the file's account of the front's movement

options.text: The landing was intended to put troops on the northern border of the country
options.misconception: Reverses the purpose and location of the landing

options.text: Supply lines played no part in the conduct of the campaign
options.misconception: Contradicts the stated purpose of the landing

questions.explanation: A landing placed behind the advancing line makes sense as an attempt to reach the enemy's supply routes rather than to extend the front, and a landing on the northern border would be the reverse of the file's description.
questions.hint: Ask what the landing was behind the line for.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compute a per-person annual aid rate from totals and population
questions.stem: A planning memo tabulates aid of 200 million dollars in the first year, 250 million in the second, and 300 million in the third for a country of 20 million people. What was the average aid per person per year?

options.text: 12.5 dollars a year, since 750 million over three years works out to 250 million a year
10 dollars a year, since 600 million over three years would give 10 each
options.misconception: Uses figures that do not match the memo

options.text: 15 dollars a year, since 900 million over three years would give 15 each
options.misconception: Uses figures that do not match the memo

options.text: 250 dollars a year, since the annual average alone is 250 million
options.misconception: Stops at the annual total without dividing by population

questions.explanation: The three years total 750 million dollars, so the annual average is 250 million, and 250 million spread over 20 million people is 12.5 dollars each per year. Skipping either the division by years or the division by people would give a different and wrong rate.
questions.hint: Total the three years, average them, then divide by population.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read a contemporary statement for the character of a long operation

stimulus.body: The transcript records a western official saying that the city has been supplied throughout the winter, that flights continued without a break, and that the operation is an exercise of patience rather than a stunt. He adds that the airlift has cost more than anyone expected.

questions.stem: What is the official's point in this passage?

options.text: That sustaining a supply over months, not a single dramatic action, was what decided the outcome
That the operation depended entirely on a single fleet of aircraft
options.misconception: Contradicts the idea of a sustained supply effort

options.text: That the airlift could be ended as soon as the weather improved
options.misconception: Contradicts the passage about patience and duration

options.text: That the blockade's effects were felt only lightly by the city's residents
options.misconception: Contradicts the supply effort the transcript describes

questions.explanation: The emphasis on continuous flights through the winter and on patience presents endurance as the decisive quality, which is a statement about duration rather than about any one sortie. The transcript also concedes real cost, so it claims neither cheapness nor a single decisive flight.
questions.hint: Listen to what the official says the operation required in time.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a recovery program achieved for the recipient countries
questions.stem: A briefing memo asks about benefits the European recovery program delivered to the participating countries themselves. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The program supplied capital and technical help at a scale that no participating government could have raised alone, and it required plans that European officials coordinated among themselves. That coordination turned national recovery efforts into a common program, and the pressure of an outside commitment often forced governments to act on projects they would otherwise have delayed. Because a large share of the money went to equipment and infrastructure rather than consumption, the aid raised the capacity of the region to produce rather than simply filling a gap in demand.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the scale of capital and coordination, the effect on the speed of projects, and the preference for productive over consumptive spending. It should avoid treating the program as a simple transfer of consumption.
questions.hint: Separate the capital, the coordination, and the timing effects.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Weigh an alliance's deterrent record against its cost
questions.stem: The city planner's memo reviews the alliance's record and what it cost its members. Which combined judgment is most accurate?

options.text: It deterred attack on its members for decades, at a steady defense cost that the members shared
It deterred nothing at all, since no attack was ever attempted against any member
options.misconception: Reasons from an absence of attacks rather than from deterrence

options.text: It raised defense costs so sharply that the weaker members left the alliance
options.misconception: Contradicts the alliance's continued membership

options.text: It produced no shared burden, since each member paid entirely for its own forces
options.misconception: Denies the sharing the alliance was built to produce

questions.explanation: Avoiding an attack on alliance members is evidence that the collective commitment changed the calculation of a potential aggressor, and the cost of that protection was carried jointly rather than alone. No attempt is not proof of no deterrence, and members did not withdraw.
questions.hint: Ask what the absence of attack shows and who paid.
